chapter_summary:
After understanding troubleshooting methodologies, it's time to apply them to specific, common network issues. One of the most frequent problems is **no connectivity**. This often points to a Layer 1 (Physical) or Layer 2 (Data Link) issue. Begin by checking the physical connection: Is the cable plugged in securely? Is the link light on the network card and switch port illuminated? If not, try a different cable or port. Verify the network interface card (NIC) is enabled and drivers are up to date. If physical connectivity seems fine, move to Layer 2. Check for MAC address table issues on switches or VLAN misconfigurations. You can use `ipconfig` or `ifconfig` to verify the NIC's status and assigned IP address. If no IP address is assigned, or it's an APIPA address (169.254.x.x), it points to a DHCP issue.

**Intermittent connectivity** can be more challenging to diagnose as the problem comes and goes. This often suggests physical layer issues like a faulty cable, loose connection, or electromagnetic interference (EMI). Wireless networks are particularly susceptible to intermittent issues due to signal interference from other devices, physical obstructions, or channel saturation. Tools like a cable tester can identify breaks or shorts in Ethernet cables. For Wi-Fi, a Wi-Fi analyzer can help identify channel conflicts or weak signal areas. Duplex mismatches (one side set to full-duplex, the other to half-duplex) can also cause intermittent connectivity and severe performance degradation, often manifesting as high collision rates on the interface. Always ensure both sides of a link are configured for the same duplex setting, preferably auto-negotiation.

**IP addressing problems** are another common source of headaches. If a device fails to obtain an IP address from a DHCP server, it might fall back to an APIPA address, preventing communication outside its local subnet. Troubleshooting involves checking the DHCP server's availability, scope configuration, and any IP helper addresses on routers. For statically configured IPs, double-check the IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway for typos. **IP conflicts** occur when two devices on the same network are assigned the same IP address. This can lead to erratic connectivity for both devices. Operating systems often detect this and alert the user. Resolution involves identifying the conflicting devices (often via MAC address) and reconfiguring one of them.

**DNS resolution failures** prevent users from accessing resources by name, even if they can reach them by IP address. If `ping 8.8.8.8` works but `ping google.com` fails, the problem is almost certainly DNS. Check the client's configured DNS servers (`ipconfig /all` or `/etc/resolv.conf`). Ensure these DNS servers are reachable (`ping <DNS_server_IP>`). If the DNS server itself is the issue, you might need to troubleshoot the DNS server service, its zone files, or its forwarders. The `nslookup` (Windows) or `dig` (Linux/macOS) commands are powerful tools for testing DNS resolution directly. For example, `nslookup google.com` will query your configured DNS server for Google's IP address.

**Slow network performance** can be caused by a multitude of factors, from bandwidth saturation to hardware limitations. Begin by establishing a baseline (as discussed in Chapter 6.1) to understand what "normal" performance looks like. Then, monitor key metrics like bandwidth utilization, latency, and packet loss. Tools like `netstat` can show active connections consuming bandwidth. If a specific application is slow, it might be an application-layer problem rather than a network one. However, if all network traffic is slow, investigate potential bottlenecks: overloaded routers/switches, insufficient bandwidth on WAN links, or even faulty NICs. Packet sniffers like Wireshark (conceptually, as a full dive is beyond Network+) can capture and analyze network traffic, revealing excessive retransmissions, high latency, or unexpected protocols consuming bandwidth. This allows you to see exactly what's happening on the wire.

Safety Note: When troubleshooting physical layer issues, especially in data centers or wiring closets, always be mindful of electrical safety. Ensure proper grounding, avoid working on live equipment without proper training, and be aware of trip hazards from cables. Labeling cables clearly can prevent accidental disconnections or misconfigurations.

screens.title: Common Network Issues and Resolution
screens.subtitle: Systematic troubleshooting for connectivity, addressing, DNS, and physical faults

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on the practical steps that help you find and fix the most common network problems you will see in the field. You will learn how to identify total loss of connectivity, intermittent connections, and slow performance, and then trace those symptoms to likely layers — physical, data link, IP addressing, or DNS. I'll explain how APIPA reveals a DHCP failure, how duplex mismatches show up as collisions, and how simple command-line tools can confirm whether the issue is DNS or deeper in the network. You will also learn the conceptual value of packet sniffing and the safety concerns when working in wiring closets or data centers. Throughout, examples use real commands and expected outputs so you can follow the same diagnostic sequence in your own environment. By the end, you will be able to gather the right evidence, select the correct tool — from a cable tester to nslookup — and resolve common misconfigurations with confidence. As you learn, ask yourself: what single test will quickly rule out the most likely layer for this symptom?

keyIdea.title: Chapter Focus
keyIdea.text: Practical diagnostics: find whether the problem is physical, link, IP addressing, DNS, or performance, then apply targeted tools and fixes.

Common Network Issues and Resolution

Why this matters

Network faults cause downtime and lost productivity. A repeatable troubleshooting flow reduces mean time to repair and prevents repeated misconfigurations.

What you'll practice

DNS failures

Performance

Visual concept

screens.title: No connectivity triage
screens.subtitle: A repeatable, layer-by-layer process to find complete loss of network access

narration.text: When a device reports no connectivity, use a simple triage sequence that rapidly eliminates likely layers. Start at the physical layer: confirm the cable is seated and link lights are present. A dark link light suggests a physical fault—test with a spare cable and another switch port. If the link light is on, verify the NIC is enabled and drivers are functional using ipconfig or ifconfig to show the interface state and the assigned IP. An APIPA address in the 169.254 range signals DHCP failure; if the interface has a valid IP in the expected subnet, move to Layer 2. At Layer 2, check VLAN membership and the switch MAC address table to ensure the port is forwarding traffic for that VLAN. If VLANs are correct, verify the default gateway is reachable by pinging the gateway IP by address. Each step eliminates a layer; you should only change configuration settings after confirming the layer above is reachable. A common misconception is to jump straight to complex logs; instead, gather simple evidence first—link light, IP address, and gateway reachability—then escalate to server or switch logs. Practice this sequence until it becomes automatic so you can isolate the fault quickly.

keyIdea.title: Triage Sequence
keyIdea.text: Physical → Interface state → VLAN/MAC table → Gateway reachability. Collect evidence at each stage before reconfiguring.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › No connectivity triage
Core Concept

No connectivity triage

A stepwise checklist to eliminate physical, link, IP, and gateway causes.

Step 1: Physical checks
Check link lights, swap cables, try another switch port, and confirm NIC is enabled.
Step 2: Interface state
Use ipconfig or ifconfig to confirm an IP address and interface status.
Step 3: Layer 2 checks
Verify VLAN assignment and MAC table entries on the switch.
Step 4: Layer 3 gateway
Ping the default gateway by IP to prove routing beyond the host.
Key Takeaway

Progress from physical to higher layers and collect simple evidence at each step to avoid misguided changes.

Example terminal checks
C:\> ipconfig /all
Ethernet adapter Local Area Connection:
   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : example.local
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . : 169.254.10.15
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.0.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . :

# A 169.254.x.x address indicates APIPA; the client could not reach DHCP.
Common mistake
Restarting services before verifying link lights often wastes time. Verify physical evidence first.
Pro tip
Label cables and test with a known-good cable when possible to rule out intermittent faults quickly.

screens.title: Layer 2 issues: VLANs and MAC tables
screens.subtitle: When frames don't get forwarded — common switch-level faults and how to find them

narration.text: Layer 2 problems prevent frames from reaching the right device even if the physical link is up. Two common causes are incorrect VLAN membership and stale or missing MAC address table entries on switches. If a port is in the wrong VLAN, the host’s frames are isolated from its subnet and will not reach the gateway. Similarly, if a switch’s MAC table does not have the client’s MAC on the expected port, traffic may be flooded or dropped. To diagnose, confirm the port’s VLAN configuration on the switch and inspect the MAC address table for the client MAC. Use show mac address-table or the equivalent on managed switches, and confirm the host’s MAC via ipconfig or ifconfig. A misconception is to assume the switch always learns correctly; static or port-security settings may prevent learning. Another real-world cause is incorrect trunk configuration between switches, which breaks VLAN propagation. When you verify the switch-side configuration and confirm the host’s MAC and VLAN, you can either correct the VLAN assignment or investigate trunking misconfigurations. This keeps troubleshooting focused and prevents unnecessary host changes.

keyIdea.title: Switch-level checks
keyIdea.text: Verify VLAN assignment and MAC table entries. Ensure trunks carry the VLAN and port security isn’t blocking MAC learning.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › VLANs & MAC tables
Definition

Layer 2 issues: VLANs and MAC tables

Frames are forwarded by VLAN and MAC learning. Misconfigurations here block traffic despite an active link.

Check VLAN membership
Ensure the access port is assigned to the expected VLAN and that trunk ports carry that VLAN between switches.
Inspect MAC table
Use switch commands to find where the host MAC is learned. Missing entries indicate a forwarding problem.
Example symptom
Host has correct IP but cannot reach other hosts in the subnet; investigate VLAN mismatch or isolated port.
Quick checks & commands
# On the switch (example syntax varies by vendor)
show vlan brief
show mac address-table | include 

# On the host
ipconfig /all   # or ifconfig
If the switch shows the MAC on a different port, investigate port moves or duplicated MACs caused by virtualization or bridging.

screens.title: Intermittent connectivity: causes and tools
screens.subtitle: How to identify transient faults from physical damage, interference, and misconfiguration

narration.text: Intermittent connectivity is challenging because the failure appears and disappears. Begin by gathering when the problem occurs and what changed recently. Physical causes include damaged cables, loose connectors, or electromagnetic interference. Wireless networks may suffer from channel saturation, competing devices, or physical obstruction. Duplex mismatch can create symptoms that look intermittent: one side in half-duplex will generate collisions and retransmissions under load. Tools you should reach for are a cable tester for wired links and a Wi‑Fi analyzer for wireless environments. A packet sniffer can capture the moment of failure to show retransmissions or sequence gaps, but only after you've narrowed the scope. A common misconception is to assume software updates caused intermittent drops; while possible, always confirm the physical layer first because swapping a cable or reseating a connector often fixes the issue. Also document the times and the pattern — consistent times suggest outside interference or scheduled traffic; random patterns suggest hardware or environmental faults. Intermittent connectivity: causes and tools means collect timing and pattern, test cables and connectors, use cable or wi‑fi analyzers, and consider duplex mismatch as a load-dependent fault.. In practical terms, how to identify transient faults from physical damage, interference, and misconfiguration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Intermittent checklist
keyIdea.text: Collect timing and pattern, test cables and connectors, use cable or Wi‑Fi analyzers, and consider duplex mismatch as a load-dependent fault.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Intermittent connectivity

Intermittent connectivity: causes

  • Physical damage: broken pair, loose terminations, or intermittent connector contact.
  • Electromagnetic Interference (EMI): motors, fluorescent lights, or nearby transmitters.
  • Wireless issues: channel overlap, signal fading, or client movement.
  • Duplex mismatch: symptoms worsen under load and cause collisions.
Tool: cable tester
Detect opens, shorts, and split pairs on Ethernet runs.
Tool: Wi‑Fi analyzer
Identify channel congestion and signal strength issues.
Example scenario
Users report short drops every few minutes. The pattern aligns with an automated device nearby switching on. A Wi‑Fi scan shows a burst of traffic on the same channel during drops, confirming interference. Changing the AP channel or moving the interfering device resolves the issue.
Common mistake

Replacing network equipment before verifying environmental interference often results in wasted hardware swaps.

screens.title: Duplex mismatch
screens.subtitle: Why mismatched duplex settings cause collisions and poor throughput

narration.text: A duplex mismatch occurs when two ends of an Ethernet link use different duplex modes — one set to full-duplex and the other to half-duplex. Full-duplex allows simultaneous send and receive, while half-duplex uses collision detection and cannot send and receive at the same time. When one side expects full-duplex while the other uses half, frames collide and are retransmitted, producing high collision rates and severe performance degradation that often looks like intermittent or slow connectivity. You can spot this in interface statistics: a spike in collisions, late collisions, or excessive retransmissions suggests duplex asymmetry. The preferred remedy is to set both ends to auto-negotiate; if auto-negotiation fails due to older hardware, explicitly configure both sides to the same speed and duplex. A common misconception is to set one side to full-duplex and leave the other to auto; this can lock the link into a mismatch. Always prefer auto-negotiation first, then match explicit settings if required. The key takeaway: duplex mismatches are a link-level misconfiguration with performance symptoms under load. Duplex mismatch means mismatched duplex leads to collisions and retransmissions; fix by matching negotiation settings on both sides.. In practical terms, why mismatched duplex settings cause collisions and poor throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Duplex mismatch impact
keyIdea.text: Mismatched duplex leads to collisions and retransmissions; fix by matching negotiation settings on both sides.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Duplex mismatch

Duplex mismatch

Different duplex settings on either end of a link cause collisions and retransmits under load, reducing effective throughput.

Symptoms
High collision counts, late collisions, and slow throughput that worsens with traffic.
Fix
Prefer auto-negotiation on both sides; if required, set identical speed and duplex manually on both devices.
Check your understanding

If collisions drop to near zero after matching settings, you have resolved a duplex mismatch.

Example interface stats
Interface GigabitEthernet0/1
  Full-duplex?      : Yes
  Collisions        : 0

Interface FastEthernet0/2
  Full-duplex?      : No
  Collisions        : 1245

# Mismatch between these two ends causes the observed collisions.

screens.title: DHCP failures and APIPA
screens.subtitle: How to detect a DHCP failure and the meaning of 169.254.x.x addresses

narration.text: Devices configured for DHCP will assign themselves an APIPA address in the 169.254.0.0/16 range when they fail to reach a DHCP server. Seeing such an address is a strong indicator that the client did not receive an address lease. Your first steps are physical verification and then checking DHCP server reachability. Use ipconfig /all or cat /etc/resolv. conf and network status commands to show the assigned IP. Next, confirm the DHCP server is reachable by pinging its IP and verify the server process and scope have available addresses. If the DHCP server is on a different subnet, ensure routers have IP helper addresses to forward requests. On Windows, release and renew the address to test: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew. If the renew fails, capture the DHCP exchange on the server or use logs to see why the lease was denied. A practical misconception is to assume the DHCP server must be down; often the issue is a full scope, missing helper, or network segmentation. Collect evidence: client IP, DHCP server reachability, and server scope health before applying changes. DHCP failures and APIPA means 169.254.x.x addresses mean the host did not receive a dhcp lease; test server reachability and scope availability next.. In practical terms, how to detect a dhcp failure and the meaning of 169.254.x.x addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: APIPA indicates DHCP issue
keyIdea.text: 169.254.x.x addresses mean the host did not receive a DHCP lease; test server reachability and scope availability next.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › DHCP & APIPA

DHCP failures and APIPA

APIPA (169.254.x.x) appears when DHCP leasing fails. Confirm reachability to DHCP server and scope availability before reconfiguring clients.

Commands to try
# Windows example
C:\> ipconfig /all
# Look for IPv4 Address or 169.254.x.x and DHCP Server entry

C:\> ipconfig /release
C:\> ipconfig /renew

# Linux example
$ ip addr show
$ sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager
Checklist
  • Verify link light and cable.
  • Ping the DHCP server IP to confirm reachability.
  • Check DHCP scope for available addresses and lease exhaustion.
  • If necessary, confirm IP helper addresses on routers for cross-subnet DHCP.
Key Takeaway

APIPA is a signal, not a solution. It tells you where to look: DHCP reachability and server scope health.

screens.title: Static IP misconfigurations vs IP conflicts
screens.subtitle: How to tell a bad static configuration from two devices using the same IP

narration.text: Static IP misconfigurations and IP conflicts both cause connectivity problems, but they have different causes and evidence. A static misconfiguration typically manifests as incorrect subnet mask or gateway settings causing the host to be unable to reach devices outside its perceived local network. In contrast, an IP conflict occurs when two devices are assigned the same IP address, either manually or by rogue DHCP assignments, leading to erratic connectivity for both devices. To differentiate them, first check the client's IP, subnet mask, and gateway for typographical errors; correct entries that do not match the network plan indicate a static misconfiguration. If the configuration appears correct but the device reports intermittent connectivity or the OS warns of a duplicate IP, scan the network for duplicate IPs and correlate MAC addresses to identify the conflicting device. Many operating systems will raise an alert when they detect another device using the same IP. When you find both devices, reconfigure one to a free address or update the DHCP reservation. A common misconception is to assume DHCP always prevents conflicts; misaligned static entries or overlapping DHCP scopes can still cause duplicate addresses, so always verify both static and DHCP allocations when resolving conflicts.

keyIdea.title: Conflict vs misconfig
keyIdea.text: Check configuration first for typos. If settings are correct but duplicates appear, identify the conflicting MAC and reassign the address or update DHCP reservations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Static vs Conflict
Static IP misconfiguration
  • Symptoms: correct IP but wrong mask/gateway prevents reaching other subnets.
  • Check: validate IP, subnet mask, and default gateway against network plan.
  • Fix: correct the static settings or convert to DHCP if appropriate.
IP conflict
  • Symptoms: intermittent connectivity, OS duplicate IP warning, erratic behavior.
  • Check: scan the network for duplicate IPs and map MAC addresses to devices.
  • Fix: change one device's address or update DHCP reservations to prevent reuse.
Example command
# Find the MAC for an IP using ARP table on a router or host
C:\> arp -a

# Use switch MAC table to locate physical port for that MAC
show mac address-table | include

screens.title: DNS resolution failures and tools
screens.subtitle: Using ping, nslookup, and dig to separate name resolution from reachability

narration.text: DNS failures often look like a network problem because users cannot reach sites by name even though IP-level connectivity works. The key diagnostic is to ping a public IP such as 8.8.8.8. If the IP ping succeeds but a domain name fails, the issue is DNS. On the client, inspect configured DNS servers with ipconfig /all or /etc/resolv. conf. Next, confirm the DNS server itself is reachable by pinging its IP. To directly test resolution, use nslookup on Windows or dig on Unix-like systems. For example, nslookup google. com will query your configured DNS server and show the returned IP. If that fails, try nslookup google. com 8.8.8.8 to force a query to a known public server; a successful result indicates a problem with the configured DNS server. If both fail, the problem may be upstream or the client configuration. A common misconception is to assume DNS caching is always to blame. While caching can cause stale answers, inability to resolve names despite IP reachability points you immediately to DNS server reachability and configuration. Document the server responses and determine whether the failure is client-side, local DNS, or broader internet DNS.

keyIdea.title: DNS triage
keyIdea.text: Confirm IP reachability first; use nslookup or dig and force queries to alternate servers to isolate local DNS issues from external resolution problems.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › DNS resolution

DNS resolution failures and tools

Use IP-level tests then name queries to determine whether DNS is the root cause.

# Basic checks
C:\> ping 8.8.8.8        # tests IP reachability
C:\> ping google.com     # tests name resolution + reachability

# Query DNS directly
C:\> nslookup google.com
C:\> nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8   # force query to Google's public DNS

# On Linux
$ dig @8.8.8.8 google.com
Practical example
If ping 8.8.8.8 succeeds but nslookup google.com fails against your local DNS and succeeds against 8.8.8.8, the local DNS server is likely misconfigured or unreachable for forwarders.
Misconception

An application error does not always mean DNS is fine. Verify by resolving names directly with nslookup or dig before blaming the app.

screens.title: DNS troubleshooting walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Follow this step sequence to determine whether DNS or network reachability is at fault

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical DNS troubleshooting sequence you can follow on a help-desk ticket. First, confirm the user can reach hosts by IP. Run ping to a known public IP, for example 8.8.8.8; a successful reply shows basic routing is intact. Second, check the client’s DNS settings with ipconfig /all or by inspecting /etc/resolv. conf to note configured DNS servers. Third, ping the primary DNS server IP to ensure reachability. Fourth, run nslookup for an internal hostname such as intranet. local. If nslookup fails, run nslookup again forcing a public server, for example nslookup google. com 8.8.8.8. If the forced query succeeds while the default fails, the local DNS or its forwarders are at fault. If both queries fail, the problem is broader: DNS server unreachable or client misconfigured. Lastly, use the results to decide whether to restart DNS services, check zone files, or correct client DNS entries. A concrete example: if the client’s DNS server is 192.168.1.1 and nslookup google. com 8.8.8.8 succeeds but nslookup google. com without the server fails, escalate to the DNS administrator with the evidence. Ask: does the DNS server forward external requests correctly?

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough conclusion
keyIdea.text: Resolve by proving IP reachability, checking client DNS settings, testing server reachability, and forcing queries to alternate DNS servers to isolate the failing component.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › DNS Walkthrough

Scenario: name resolution fails, IP succeeds

Follow these steps to determine whether the problem is client, local DNS server, or upstream DNS.

Step 1: Verify IP reachability
ping 8.8.8.8 — if this works, network routing is likely fine.
Step 2: Check DNS configuration
ipconfig /all or cat /etc/resolv.conf to list configured DNS servers.
Step 3: Test DNS server reachability
ping the DNS server IP to ensure it’s reachable from the client.
Step 4: Use nslookup/dig
nslookup intranet.local then nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8 to force a public query.
Expected outputs
# Example failing nslookup
C:\> nslookup intranet.local
*** Can't find intranet.local: No response from server

# Example forced success
C:\> nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8
Server:  google-public-dns-a.google.com
Address:  8.8.8.8

Name:    google.com
Address: 142.250.190.142

screens.title: Slow network performance: baseline and metrics
screens.subtitle: How to separate application issues from network bottlenecks using simple metrics

narration.text: When users complain about slow performance, it's crucial to determine whether the network or the application is the cause. Start with a baseline of normal performance — typical bandwidth, latency, and packet loss for the network — so you know what 'slow' means. Monitor current metrics: bandwidth utilization, interface errors, latency (ping), and packet loss. Tools like netstat can show active connections consuming bandwidth. If only one application is slow while others are normal, the issue may be at the application layer. If all traffic is slow, inspect for saturated links, overloaded routers, or hardware limitations on NICs or switches. Packet captures can reveal retransmissions and unexpected protocols consuming bandwidth; excessive retransmissions indicate packet loss causing slow throughput. A common pitfall is to assume more bandwidth solves the problem; sometimes the root cause is a misbehaving application or a faulty NIC producing retransmits. Collecting objective metrics guides whether you upgrade capacity or troubleshoot the application or hardware. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Slow performance

Slow network performance

Measure bandwidth, latency, and packet loss and compare to a known baseline to find where the bottleneck lies.

Useful indicators
  • High interface utilization: indicates saturated link.
  • High latency and packet loss: could suggest congestion or faulty links.
  • Excessive retransmissions in captures: suggests packet loss or errors on the media.
# Check active connections and listening sockets
C:\> netstat -anob

# Monitor interface counters on a switch or router for errors and utilization
show interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Real-world connection
If peak business hours show slow performance, compare utilization graphs to off-peak periods. If spikes match business processes, plan capacity or traffic shaping; if not, investigate faulty hardware or misbehaving applications.

narration.text: Packet sniffing captures traffic on the wire so you can inspect packet-level behavior. While a full Wireshark deep-dive is beyond this chapter, understanding the concept helps you identify clear signs: excessive retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgements, or protocols consuming unexpected bandwidth. A capture showing many retransmissions suggests packet loss or faulty links, while unexpected protocol types might reveal misconfigured services or a rogue application. Use sniffers conceptually: plan the capture, avoid collecting sensitive data, and focus on short windows around the failure symptom to reduce noise. Always follow organizational policies when capturing traffic. An important misconception is that packet capture always points to a single root cause; captures are diagnostic evidence that must be correlated with other findings like interface errors or application logs. The practical use is to confirm whether retransmits originate on the LAN or over a WAN link, guiding you toward either local hardware fixes or further capacity planning. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Packet sniffing (conceptual)

Packet sniffing — what to look for

  • Retransmissions and duplicate ACKs indicating packet loss.
  • Unexpected protocols or large flows using bandwidth.
  • Traffic patterns that correlate with performance degradation times.
Keep captures short and focused to reduce sensitive data exposure. Document why you captured and what you found so that fixes are evidence-driven.
Ethics & safety
Only capture with authorization and within policy. Avoid storing or analyzing private user content when not necessary for troubleshooting.

narration.text: Here are the most important concepts to remember. APIPA tells you the client failed to get a DHCP lease. Duplex mismatch causes collisions and poor performance when ends of a link use different duplex modes. An IP conflict occurs when two devices share the same IP and causes erratic connectivity. Use nslookup or dig to query DNS servers and separate name resolution problems from IP reachability. Packet sniffers let you inspect retransmissions and unexpected protocols but must be used carefully. Finally, electromagnetic interference can cause intermittent drops and should always be considered for wired and wireless troubleshooting. These compact reminders map directly to diagnostic steps you use in the field: verify link lights, confirm IP addressing, test DNS queries, and gather packet-level evidence when needed. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts
APIPA
169.254.x.x address indicates DHCP lease failure; test server reachability and scope.
Duplex Mismatch
Different duplex modes cause collisions and retransmits; match negotiation settings.
IP Conflict
Two devices with the same IP lead to erratic connectivity; map MACs to resolve.

narration.text: Continue to carry these quick reminders into your troubleshooting: use nslookup and dig to force DNS queries and to determine whether the configured server is the problem. Packet sniffers let you see retransmissions and unexpected traffic but must be used with care. Electromagnetic interference can affect both wired and wireless links and should be suspected for intermittent problems that correlate with nearby equipment. Keep these concepts as a mental map: quick IP test, DNS query, link and interface stats, then packet capture if needed. These steps will help you reduce guesswork and base your fixes on clear evidence. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts
nslookup / dig
Force queries to specific servers to isolate local DNS problems from upstream issues.
Packet sniffer
Use captures to confirm retransmissions, high latency, and bandwidth patterns when other checks point to network-level causes.
EMI
Consider electromagnetic interference for intermittent faults, and test with a different cable route or shielded cabling.
Final takeaway

Start with simple tests that reveal the layer at fault, gather evidence, then apply targeted fixes. Repeatable diagnosis reduces downtime and avoids unnecessary changes.
